title: Test anxiety and stamina
lines: Almost everyone feels nervous about the GRE. A little nervousness helps you focus. Too much makes you read the same sentence three times, forget a formula you know well or rush through easy questions. The good news is that both anxiety and stamina respond to training, just like vocabulary or algebra.
## Why the test feels stressful
- It is timed, and the timer is visible.
- It matters for goals you care about.
- It adapts, so a hard section can feel like failure even when it means you did well.
- There is no scheduled break, so nearly two hours of focus are needed.
Knowing these reasons helps. When you notice the pressure, you can name it: "This is the timer stress I expected." Naming a feeling often reduces it.
## Familiarity is the best cure
Uncertainty feeds anxiety. Remove as much of it as you can before test day.
- Know the exact format, order and timing of every section. Read the format article until it feels boring.
- Take full mock tests in realistic conditions: same time of day, phone away, no pauses, essay included.
- Practice the check-in steps for at-home testing, or visit the route to your test center.
- Decide your pacing plan and checkpoints in advance, so you do not make decisions under pressure.
## A breathing reset
Use this when your mind races or you notice your shoulders are tense. It takes about 20 seconds.
> Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of four.
> Hold for a count of two.
> Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of six.
> Repeat twice, then reread the question from the start.
Practice it during mock tests so it is automatic on the day.
## Thoughts that help
- "One question is worth very little. I can let this one go."
- "Hard questions mean I am probably doing well."
- "I have practiced this. I know what to do next."
- "Mark, guess, move on."

Thoughts that hurt are often predictions: "I am going to fail", "Everyone else finds this easy". When you notice one, return your attention to the task in front of you: the next sentence, the next number.
! Do not try to calculate your score during the test. It takes attention away from the questions and is almost always wrong.
## Building stamina
The GRE asks for close to two hours of concentration without a break. Stamina is built gradually.
- Weeks 1-2 of your plan: study in focused blocks of 30-45 minutes.
- Middle weeks: extend to blocks of 60-75 minutes, such as two sections back to back.
- Final weeks: take full mock tests, about 2 hours, at least once a week.
- Train on paper or screen the same way you will test, including your note-taking material.
## The body matters
- Sleep: keep a regular sleep time for the last two weeks. One late night of revision does more harm than good.
- Food: eat a normal meal one to two hours before the test. Avoid trying a new food or drink that day.
- Caffeine: if you usually drink coffee or tea, have your normal amount; do not double it.
- Movement: a short walk before the test can lower tension.
## During the test
- Between sections, sit back, breathe slowly once and drop your shoulders.
- If you feel your focus slipping in a long passage, read one sentence at a time and summarize it in a few words.
- If you blank on a formula, write down what you do know. Often the rest comes back.
- If one section goes badly, treat the next one as a fresh start. Sections are scored separately.
## When anxiety is very strong

If test anxiety often stops you from working, even in practice, talk to someone you trust, a teacher or a counselor. Support is a normal part of preparing for an important exam. If you have a documented condition, ETS offers testing accommodations; read the details and the request process on ets.org early, because it can take time.
## Using the app for confidence
- Start with practice sets on your strongest topic to build momentum, then move to a weak one.
- Watch your Progress tab. Seeing accuracy rise week by week is real evidence that you are improving.
- Take your mocks seriously but kindly. A low score in week 2 is information, not a verdict.
- Before the real test, look back at your first mock result. You have already come a long way.
